title: The wells of Badr
hook: a small, outnumbered band of Muslims meets the Meccan army by the wells of Badr, and wins

segments.voice: Yesterday, kutiba, the first Ramadan in Medina. Your line was prescribed for you. Did you put a fast day on your calendar? Day two hundred sixty-four.

It's that same first Ramadan. And word comes that a large army has marched out of Mecca, the city that drove them out, about a thousand men, with horses and armor. The Muslims who ride out to meet them number a little over three hundred. The biographers say they have two horses between them, and about seventy camels, taking turns riding. Some have no armor at all. They camp near a group of wells in a valley called Badr, on the caravan road southwest of Medina. The night before, it rains. The next morning, the two sides face each other across the sand. Today: Badr.
screen: `A THOUSAND FROM MECCA.` → `THREE HUNDRED AND SOME.` → `A VALLEY OF WELLS.`

segments.voice: Two moments before the battle are worth knowing. The first is about the wells, and it comes from the early biographer Ibn Ishaq. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ stopped the army at one spot. A companion named al-Hubab ibn al-Mundhir came to him and asked, politely: is this place one God has shown you, or is it your own judgment, a matter of war and planning? The Prophet said it was his own judgment. Then, said al-Hubab, this isn't the right place. Let's move to the well nearest the enemy, build a cistern, and keep the water on our side. And the Prophet said: you've given good advice, and moved the whole army. A prophet, taking correction from a soldier, in front of everyone. The second moment is the night. Sahih Muslim describes the Prophet standing in prayer, hands raised, calling on God so long and so hard that his cloak slipped off his shoulders, and Abu Bakr put it back and told him, enough, God will keep his promise to you. Then the battle. The Meccans broke. Sahih al-Bukhari counts seventy of them killed and seventy taken captive, among the dead several of the leaders who had tormented the Muslims in Mecca. The biographers name about fourteen Muslims who died. The Qur'an looks back on it later: God had already helped you at Badr, when you were weak and few. It says the Muslims were strengthened with angels, and it says the victory was God's, not theirs. Muslim teachers often tell Badr not as a story about strength, but about the opposite: how little they had, and how much came through anyway.
screen: `YOUR JUDGMENT, OR GOD'S?` · `MOVE TO THE NEAREST WELL.` · `HIS CLOAK SLIPPED IN PRAYER.` · `WHEN YOU WERE WEAK AND FEW.` · then, large: `FEW AGAINST MANY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember an unlikely rescue. Sit, and go back in your own life to a time when the odds were against you. Not enough money, not enough time, not enough strength. And somehow, you got through. A stranger's help. A door that opened at the last minute. Let the memory come back in detail: where you were, what you felt. Then notice how little you actually had then. If you pray, you can thank God for it. The bell holds the time.
Badr, the valley where a small, outnumbered band of Muslims met the Meccan army in the first Ramadan, and won.
Your line: few against many. Today, when something feels too big for what you've got, remember the three hundred, and take the next step anyway. Day two hundred sixty-four.

howItsDone: Some Muslims mark the battle of Badr in Ramadan with talks in mosques about the people who took part, whom later generations honored as the people of Badr.

fork.setup: you're a companion. the Prophet has chosen a spot for the army, but you think it's a bad one. what do you do?
options: ask if it's revelation or his own judgment, then advise.
move your own tent without telling anyone.
fork.reveal: al-Hubab asked, heard it was the Prophet's judgment, and advised the nearest well. the Prophet said: good advice, and moved everyone.

original.note: Arabic: Badr, the valley and its wells. the word also means a full moon.

trapdoor: what you thought: a famous battle.
what it means: the first Ramadan's battle, three hundred against a thousand, remembered for how little the Muslims had.
what a scholar hears: al-Hubab's question separates revelation from the Prophet's own judgment in worldly matters, a distinction scholars built on later.

sources.ref: Qur'an 3:123 (God helped you at Badr when you were weak)

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: cut 'many are fasting' (a report in at-Tirmidhi says they broke the fast on the Badr march) and the unsourced 17 Ramadan date; attributed the al-Hubab story to Ibn Ishaq and the horses/camels and Muslim dead to the biographers; casualty count now cites Bukhari 3986; softened 'Muslims have remembered Badr ever since'.
Numbers (about 313 Muslims; about 950–1,000 Meccans; two horses, seventy camels; about seventy Meccans and fourteen Muslims killed) follow the standard sirah; confirm.
The al-Hubab episode is from Ibn Ishaq and is considered weak in its chain by some hadith scholars; told as the sirah tells it. Confirm framing.
War content: kept factual, no glorification. Keeper to confirm tone.
'Badr also means a full moon': true of the common noun; the valley's name is often explained by a man named Badr who dug the well. Confirm the note.
